summary: Defines a MIB to configure, monitor, and control a service interworking function for permanent virtual circuits between Frame Relay and ATM technologies.

plainLanguage.summary: Two older kinds of network lines speak different languages. This lets tools manage the translator between them.

questions: frame relay to atm pvc management
what is the frame relay atm interworking mib
how to create a frame relay to atm pvc cross-connect
what snmp objects manage frame relay atm interworking
subtitle: An SNMP MIB for setting up, watching and controlling the box that links Frame Relay circuits to ATM circuits.

tldr.problem: A Frame Relay/ATM service interworking function connects a Frame Relay permanent virtual circuit to an ATM one, but operators had no standard SNMP objects to provision, monitor and control it.
tldr.mechanism: The MIB adds a cross-connect table with one row per interworked connection, a connection description table that holds shared behaviour settings, an augmentation of the ATM MIB VCL table and one status change notification.
tldr.outcome: Managers can create, activate and tear down interworked connections and read counters for translation failures. The RFC is updated by RFC 9141.

facts.label: Based on
facts.value: FRF.8 (Frame Relay Forum and ATM Forum agreements)

today: RFC 2955 is a Proposed Standard from October 2000. It has not been obsoleted, but it is updated by RFC 9141.

sections.title: What the MIB Manages
sections.content:
RFC 2955 defines a Management Information Base (MIB) for monitoring and controlling a service interworking function (IWF) for Permanent Virtual Connections (PVC) between Frame Relay and Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM). The agreements behind it were reached jointly by the Frame Relay Forum and the ATM Forum and are documented in FRF.8. The RFC itself consults FRF.8 for details of how the function operates.

Two interworking types exist for Frame Relay and ATM PVCs. Network interworking forwards data between Frame Relay users that are connected over an ATM service. Service interworking, the subject of this MIB, forwards data so that the ATM user performs no Frame Relay functions and the Frame Relay user performs no ATM functions. Optionally the function translates particular higher layer protocols. FRF.8 does not cover point-to-multipoint use, but implementations MAY support it with this MIB.

The module is written in SMIv2 and fits into the SNMP Management Framework summarized in section 1 of the RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: A Frame Relay line and an ATM line cannot talk directly. A translator sits in the middle so each side thinks it is talking to its own kind. This memo is about the remote control for that translator.

sections.title: Structure of the MIB
sections.content:
The managed objects fall into three parts: the FR/ATM PVC Service IWF cross-connect table, a connection description table and a notification object.

The cross-connect table has one or more rows for each interworked connection. A point-to-point connection uses one row. A point-to-multipoint connection uses one row per multipoint destination. The connection is identified by frAtmIwfConnIndex, and the rows are distinguished by index objects for the ATM port, VPI, VCI, Frame Relay port and DLCI.

Most connections share the same behaviour, so the settings live in the connection description table. Each row of that table holds attributes common to one or more connections. A cross-connect row points to its descriptor with frAtmIwfConnectionDescriptor. For point-to-multipoint, all rows with the same connection index MUST use the same descriptor, and they MUST agree on which side is the single one: many Frame Relay PVCs to one ATM PVC, or one Frame Relay PVC to many ATM PVCs.
sections.plainLanguage: There is one list of which line is hooked to which, and a separate list of settings cards. Many hookups can point at the same settings card, so you do not rewrite the same settings over and over.

sections.title: How It Fits With Other MIBs
sections.content:
Each PVC endpoint is still provisioned in its own technology MIB. Frame Relay endpoints are rows in the Frame Relay Service MIB endpoint table (RFC 2954), and ATM endpoints are rows in the ATM MIB virtual connection link table (RFC 2515). Interface numbers (ifIndex) come from the IF MIB (RFC 2863). The Frame Relay DTE MIB has no relevance to this MIB.

Without interworking, two endpoints of the same technology are linked in that technology's cross-connect table. With interworking, those cross-connect identifiers are set to zero. Instead, the Frame Relay endpoint's frPVCEndptAtmIwfConnIndex and the ATM endpoint's frAtmIwfVclCrossConnectIdentifier point to the row in the FR/ATM IWF cross-connect table. The latter object is defined in this MIB, in a table that augments the ATM MIB VCL table. The system sets these pointer objects as a side effect of establishing the cross-connect, so they are read-only.
sections.plainLanguage: Each end of the connection keeps its own record in its own file. When the translator joins them, both records get a sticky note that says which hookup they belong to.

sections.title: Creating, Destroying and Changing a Connection
sections.content:
Creating a cross-connection takes several steps. First rows must be created in the Frame Relay endpoint table, the ATM VCL table, the connection descriptor table and the cross-connect table. Then the new rows are cross-linked. Finally the administrative and operational status objects are set to up(1). The RFC walks through seven steps, using a manager that sends SNMP requests to an agent built into the IWF system.

To pick indexes safely, the manager reads frAtmIwfConnectionDescriptorIndexNext and frAtmIwfConnIndexNext from the agent and uses the values returned. The Frame Relay and ATM endpoints MUST exist before the cross-connect row is created, because their identifiers are part of that row's index.

To tear down, the manager sets frAtmIwfConnRowStatus to destroy(6). The agent cleans up, the endpoint pointer objects go back to zero and the ATM operational status goes to down(2). After that the manager MAY destroy the endpoint rows. Changing a connection is at the agent's discretion: leaves can be added or removed using the same procedures, but changing traffic or service category parameters requires releasing the cross-connect first.
sections.plainLanguage: Building a connection is like plugging in a phone: make the two sockets, pick a settings card, join them, then flip the switch on. Taking it down goes the other way around.

sections.title: The Connection Descriptor
sections.content:
A descriptor row sets how the IWF transforms data on the connections that use it. It covers five areas: mapping the Frame Relay discard eligibility (DE) bit to the ATM cell loss priority (CLP) bit and back, mapping congestion indication, mapping the higher-layer encapsulation, fragmentation and reassembly, and ARP translation between ATM and Frame Relay.

The mapping objects use modes from FRF.8. For example, in the Frame Relay to ATM direction mode1 copies DE to the CLP field of every cell, while mode2Const0 and mode2Const1 set CLP to a constant. The encapsulation mode can be transparentMode (forward unaltered), translationMode (map a subset) or translationModeAll. Fragmentation and ARP translation each default to disabled.

A descriptor row MUST be active(1) before any connection references it, and destroying a descriptor MUST fail while any connection still uses it.
sections.plainLanguage: A settings card says how to translate small details, like how important a message is and how to wrap it up. Mode one means copy the detail across, and others mean always say yes or always say no.

sections.title: Status, Counters and Notifications
sections.content:
Each cross-connect row has an administrative status (up(1) or down(2)), separate operational status objects for the ATM to Frame Relay and Frame Relay to ATM directions, and timestamps for the last change in each. A row can be created in one step with createAndGo(4), and before a row is destroyed the endpoints MUST be down(2).

Six read-only Counter32 objects record trouble. They count frames or PDUs that could not be translated, frames too large for AAL5 segmentation, SDUs too large for the Frame Relay side, AAL5 PDUs with CRC-32 errors, and partially reassembled PDUs discarded because reassembly timed out. In transparent mode the translation counters must return noSuchInstance.

A single notification, frAtmIwfConnStatusChange, tells the manager that the status of an interworking connection has changed. It carries the admin status and both operational status values.
sections.plainLanguage: The translator has a switch and some lights to say whether it is on, plus tally counters for things that went wrong. If the status changes, it rings a bell so the operator hears about it.

sections.title: Conformance
sections.content:
There are two compliance statements. One is for equipment and one is for a service offered through a customer network management (CNM) interface. Both require the basic connection group, the connection descriptor group, the ATM VCL augmentation group and the notifications group.

The requirements are modest. Equipment needs only mode1 for the DE, CLP and congestion mappings, and only transparent mode for encapsulation. Translation mode is optional, as are fragmentation and reassembly and ARP translation. The CNM view additionally allows most of these objects, and the row status, to be read-only.
sections.plainLanguage: A product only has to support the simple, basic settings to count as compliant. The fancy options are extras.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Several objects have read-write or read-create access and may be sensitive in some environments. Allowing SET operations without proper protection can hurt network operations. The RFC says no objects in the MIB contain sensitive information.

SNMPv1 on its own is not a secure environment. Even on a protected network, for example with IPSec, there is no control over who may GET or SET these objects. Implementers are recommended to use the SNMPv3 security features, namely the User-based Security Model (RFC 2574) and the View-based Access Control Model (RFC 2575). It is then up to the user to configure the SNMP entity so that only legitimate principals can read or change these objects.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone who could turn the knobs could break the connections, so only trusted people should get the keys.

items.title: Loss priority
items.text: Maps the ATM CLP bit to the Frame Relay DE bit, and back.

items.title: Congestion
items.text: Maps the ATM congestion notification bit to Frame Relay congestion bits.

items.title: Encapsulation
items.text: Maps higher protocol encapsulations between ATM and Frame Relay.

items.title: ARP translation
items.text: Performs ARP translation between ATM and Frame Relay.
